label: lema2
title: Lemma
body_md:
(See \cite[Lemma 2]{N}.)\label{lema2} Let $T,s\geq1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_T,y_1,\ldots,y_s\in\mathbb N_0$ satisfy
\[
 \sum_{\rho=1}^{T}2^{x_\rho}
 =
 \sum_{r=1}^{s}2^{y_r},
 \qquad
 y_1<\cdots<y_s.
\]
The $x_\rho$ need not be distinct. Then there exists a partition
\[
 \{1,\ldots,T\}=J_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup J_s
\]
such that
\[
 2^{y_r}=\sum_{\rho\in J_r}2^{x_\rho}
 \qquad(1\leq r\leq s).
\]
head: environment

label: lema3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lema3} Let
\[
 n=b_1+\cdots+b_q,
 \qquad b_\ell\in B_{j_\ell}\quad(1\leq\ell\leq q).
\]
If $n'$ is a nonnegative integer satisfying
\[
 {S}(n')\subseteq{S}(n),
\]
then there exist $b'_\ell\in B_{j_\ell}$ such that
\[
 n'=b'_1+\cdots+b'_q,
 \qquad
 {S}(b'_\ell)\subseteq{S}(b_\ell)
 \quad(1\leq\ell\leq q).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $n=0$, then $b_1=\cdots=b_q=n'=0$, and the choice
$b'_\ell=0$ proves the assertion. Hence assume $n>0$.
Write
\[
 S(n)=\{y_1,\ldots,y_s\},
 \qquad y_1<\cdots<y_s,
 \qquad n=\sum_{r=1}^{s}2^{y_r}.
\]
For every $1\leq\ell\leq q$, write
\(b_\ell=\sum_{x\in{S}(b_\ell)}2^x\).
Let
\[
 T=\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\left|{S}(b_\ell)\right|.
\]
List all the binary terms above, with multiplicities, as
\[
 2^{x_1},\ldots,2^{x_T}.
\]
Then
\[
 \sum_{\rho=1}^{T}2^{x_\rho}
 =\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}b_\ell
 =n
 =\sum_{r=1}^{s}2^{y_r}.
\]
Let $\lambda(\rho)$ denote the index of the summand containing
$2^{x_\rho}$, for $1\leq\rho\leq T$. Then, for
$1\leq\ell\leq q$,
\[
 \{x_\rho:\lambda(\rho)=\ell\}={S}(b_\ell).
\]

By Lemma~\ref{lema2}, there exists a partition
\[
 \{1,\ldots,T\}=J_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup J_s
\]
such that
\[
 2^{y_r}=\sum_{\rho\in J_r}2^{x_\rho}
 \qquad(1\leq r\leq s).
\]
By
\[
 {S}(n')\subseteq{S}(n)=\{y_1,\ldots,y_s\},
\]
let
\[
 R'=\{r\in\{1,\ldots,s\}:y_r\in{S}(n')\}.
\]
Then
\[
 n'
 =\sum_{r\in R'}2^{y_r}
 =\sum_{r\in R'}\sum_{\rho\in J_r}2^{x_\rho}.
\]
For $1\leq\ell\leq q$, define
\[
 b'_\ell
 =\sum_{r\in R'}
   \sum_{\substack{\rho\in J_r\\\lambda(\rho)=\ell}}2^{x_\rho}.
\]
For a fixed $\ell$, only some of the binary terms of $b_\ell$ are retained. Hence
\[
 {S}(b'_\ell)
 \subseteq
 \{x_\rho:\lambda(\rho)=\ell\}
 ={S}(b_\ell).
\]
Since $b_\ell\in B_{j_\ell}$ and
$S(b'_\ell)\subseteq S(b_\ell)$, we have
\[
 S(b'_\ell)\subseteq S(b_\ell)\subseteq W_{j_\ell},
 \qquad b'_\ell\in B_{j_\ell}
 \quad(1\leq\ell\leq q).
\]
Finally, since $J_1,\ldots,J_s$ are pairwise disjoint,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{\ell=1}^{q}b'_\ell
 &=\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}
   \sum_{r\in R'}
   \sum_{\substack{\rho\in J_r\\\lambda(\rho)=\ell}}2^{x_\rho}\\
 &=\sum_{r\in R'}\sum_{\rho\in J_r}2^{x_\rho}\\
 &=\sum_{r\in R'}2^{y_r}\\
 &=n'.
\end{align*}
This completes the proof of the lemma.

label: lema4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lema4} Let $M\geq1$, let $q_0,\ldots,q_{M-1}$ be nonnegative integers, and let $n$ be an integer with $0\leq n<2^M$. Then
\[
 n=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t,
 \qquad
 0\leq d_t\leq q_t,
\]
holds for some integers $d_t$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq6}
 n\bmod2^r
 \leq
 \sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t
 \qquad(1\leq r\leq M).
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that there exist integers $d_0,\ldots,d_{M-1}$ satisfying
\[
 n=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t,
 \qquad
 0\leq d_t\leq q_t.
\]
For $1\leq r\leq M$,
\begin{align*}
 n&=\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}d_t2^t
 +2^r\sum_{t=r}^{M-1}d_t2^{t-r},\\
 n\bmod2^r&=\left(\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}d_t2^t\right)\bmod2^r,\\
 0\leq n\bmod2^r
 &\leq\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}d_t2^t
 \leq\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t.
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{eq6}.

Conversely, we prove by induction on $M$ that the conditions
\begin{equation}\label{eq7}
 \left\{
 \begin{aligned}
 0&\leq n\leq\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}q_t2^t,\\
 n\bmod2^r&\leq\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t
 \qquad(1\leq r<M),
 \end{aligned}
 \right.
\end{equation}
imply the existence of integers $d_0,\ldots,d_{M-1}$ with
\[
 n=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t,
 \qquad
 0\leq d_t\leq q_t.
\]
For $M=1$, take $d_0=n\in[0,q_0]$.

Now let $M\geq2$ and assume the assertion for $M-1$. Write
\(n=Q2^{M-1}+R\),
where
\[
 Q=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{M-1}}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 0\leq R<2^{M-1}.
\]
Define
\[
 d_{M-1}=\min\{q_{M-1},Q\},
 \qquad
 n'=n-d_{M-1}2^{M-1}.
\]
Clearly,
\[
 0\leq d_{M-1}\leq q_{M-1}.
\]

If $Q\leq q_{M-1}$, then
\begin{align*}
 d_{M-1}&=Q,\\
 n'&=R=n\bmod2^{M-1},\\
 0\leq n'&\leq\sum_{t=0}^{M-2}q_t2^t
 \qquad\text{by \eqref{eq7}}.
\end{align*}
If $Q>q_{M-1}$, then
\begin{align*}
 d_{M-1}&=q_{M-1},\\
 n'&=(Q-q_{M-1})2^{M-1}+R>0,\\
 n'&=n-q_{M-1}2^{M-1}
 \leq\sum_{t=0}^{M-2}q_t2^t
 \qquad\text{by \eqref{eq7}}.
\end{align*}
In either case,
\begin{equation}\label{eq8}
 0\leq n'\leq\sum_{t=0}^{M-2}q_t2^t.
\end{equation}

Since
\(n-n'=d_{M-1}2^{M-1}\),
for every $1\leq r<M-1$, we have
\(n'\equiv n\pmod{2^r}\).
Therefore,
\[
 n'\bmod2^r
 =n\bmod2^r
 \leq
 \sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t
 \qquad(1\leq r<M-1).
\]
By \eqref{eq8} and the induction hypothesis, there exist integers
$d_0,\ldots,d_{M-2}$ such that
\[
 n'=\sum_{t=0}^{M-2}d_t2^t,
 \qquad
 0\leq d_t\leq q_t
 \quad(0\leq t<M-1).
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 n
 &=n'+d_{M-1}2^{M-1}\\
 &=\sum_{t=0}^{M-2}d_t2^t+d_{M-1}2^{M-1}\\
 &=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t,
\end{align*}
and
\[
 0\leq d_t\leq q_t
 \qquad(0\leq t<M).
\]
Thus the stronger assertion holds for every $M$. For $0\leq n<2^M$, \eqref{eq6} implies
\[
 0\leq n=n\bmod2^M\leq\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}q_t2^t,
 \qquad
 n\bmod2^r\leq\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t\quad(1\leq r<M).
\]
Applying \eqref{eq7}, we obtain
\[
 n=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t,\qquad
 0\leq d_t\leq q_t\quad(0\leq t<M).
\]

label: lema5
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an integer
\[
 M>w
\]
and a vector
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathcal K_h.
\]
For each $0\leq t<M$, since $W_1,\ldots,W_h$ partition $\mathbb N_0$, there is a unique index
\[
 c(t)\in\{1,\ldots,h\}
\]
with
\(t\in W_{c(t)}\).
Let
\(q_t=k_{c(t)} \qquad(0\leq t<M)\).

Let $0\leq n<2^M$. We first establish the equivalence
\[
 n\in\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j
 \quad\text{if and only if}\quad
 n=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t
 \quad\text{for some integers }0\leq d_t\leq q_t.
\]
Indeed, if
\(n\in\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j\),
then we may write
\[
 n=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sum_{u=1}^{k_j}b_{j,u},
 \qquad
 b_{j,u}\in B_j.
\]
Since all summands are nonnegative,
\[
 0\leq b_{j,u}\leq n<2^M,
 \qquad S(b_{j,u})\subseteq[0,M)\cap\mathbb Z.
\]
For $0\leq t<M$, define
\[
 d_t
 =\left|\{u:1\leq u\leq k_{c(t)},\ t\in{S}(b_{c(t),u})\}\right|.
\]
Since $t$ belongs to no set other than $W_{c(t)}$,
\[
 0\leq d_t\leq k_{c(t)}=q_t.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{align*}
 n
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\sum_{u=1}^{k_j}
   \sum_{t\in{S}(b_{j,u})}2^t\\
 &=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t.
\end{align*}

Conversely, suppose that there exist integers $d_t$ satisfying
\[
 n=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t,
 \qquad
 0\leq d_t\leq k_{c(t)}.
\]
For every $0\leq t<M$, choose a subset $U_t$ of
\[
 \{1,\ldots,k_{c(t)}\}
\]
with $d_t$ elements. For
$1\leq j\leq h$ and $1\leq u\leq k_j$, define
\[
 b_{j,u}
 =\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\in W_j\\u\in U_t}}2^t.
\]
By construction,
\[
 S(b_{j,u})\subseteq W_j,
 \qquad b_{j,u}\in B_j.
\]
Moreover, $|U_t|=d_t$, so
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j=1}^{h}\sum_{u=1}^{k_j}b_{j,u}
 &=\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}d_t2^t\\
 &=n.
\end{align*}
Thus
\[
 n\in\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j.
\]

By Lemma~\ref{lema4}, this representation exists if and only if
\[
 n\bmod2^r
 \leq
 \sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t
 \qquad(1\leq r\leq M).
\]
Since $q_t=k_{c(t)}$ and $t\in W_{c(t)}$, we have
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t=0}^{r-1}q_t2^t
 &=\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}k_{c(t)}2^t\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_j
   \sum_{t\in W_j\cap[0,r)}2^t\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jP_j(r).
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq11}
\begin{gathered}
n\in\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j
\quad\text{if and only if}\\[2pt]
n\bmod 2^r\leq\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jP_j(r)
\qquad(1\leq r\leq M).
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

Now take
\[
 n_M
 =2^w+\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\notin W_i}}2^t.
\]
Since $w\in W_i$ and $w<M$, the binary positions in the expression above are distinct and all are less than $M$. Hence
\[
 0<n_M\leq\sum_{t=0}^{M-1}2^t=2^M-1<2^M.
\]
Fix $1\leq r\leq M$.

If $r\leq w$, then $2^w$ is divisible by $2^r$, and hence
\begin{align*}
 n_M\bmod2^r
 &=\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<r\\t\notin W_i}}2^t\\
 &=\sum_{j\neq i}\sum_{t\in W_j\cap[0,r)}2^t\\
 &=\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r).
\end{align*}
If $r>w$, then the position $w$ remains among the lowest $r$ binary positions, and hence
\begin{align*}
 n_M\bmod2^r
 &=2^w+\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<r\\t\notin W_i}}2^t\\
 &=2^w+\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r).
\end{align*}
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq12}
 n_M\bmod2^r
 =
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r),&r\leq w,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r)+2^w,&r>w.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq11} and \eqref{eq12},
$n_M\notin\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j$ holds precisely when there is
an integer $1\leq r\leq M$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq13}
 \sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jP_j(r)
 <
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r),&r\leq w,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r)+2^w,&r>w.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}

Suppose that (a) holds. Since
\[
 \mathcal K_h
 =\{(k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}^h:
 k_1+\cdots+k_h=h\},
\]
we obtain
\[
 \left|\mathcal K_h\right|=\binom{2h-1}{h-1}<\infty.
\]
For every
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)
 \in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\},
\]
choose, by (a), an integer
\[
 t(k_1,\ldots,k_h)\geq1
\]
such that \eqref{eq9} holds. Let
\[
 M
 =\max\Bigl(
 \{w+1\}\cup
 \{t(k_1,\ldots,k_h):
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in
 \mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\}\}
 \Bigr).
\]
Then
\(M>w\).
For each such vector, take
\(r=t(k_1,\ldots,k_h)\leq M\).
By \eqref{eq9}, \eqref{eq13} holds at this value of $r$. Therefore,
\[
 n_M\notin\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j.
\]
This holds simultaneously for all
$(k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\}$
and hence (b) follows.

Conversely, suppose that (b) holds. Fix any
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)
 \in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\}.
\]
By (b),
\[
 n_M\notin\sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jB_j.
\]
By \eqref{eq13}, there exists an integer
\(1\leq r\leq M\)
such that
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{h}k_jP_j(r)
 <
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r),&r\leq w,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(r)+2^w,&r>w.
 \end{cases}
\]
Taking $t=r$ proves (a).

label: eq14
title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that conditions~(I) and~(II) hold. By condition~(I),
\begin{equation}\label{eq14}
 W_j(m)=\frac mh+O(1)
 \qquad(1\leq j\leq h).
\end{equation}
Fix
\[
 a\in A_i,
 \qquad
 w\in{S}(a)\subseteq W_i.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lema5}, there exists an integer $M>w$ such that for every
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\},
\]
we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq15}
 2^w+\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\notin W_i}}2^t
 \notin
 \sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j.
\end{equation}
The strict prefix inequality in \eqref{eq13}, once satisfied at some $r\leq M$, is independent of the choice of larger $M$. Thus the exclusion \eqref{eq15} persists when $M$ is enlarged. We may therefore also assume that
\begin{equation}\label{eq16}
 {S}(a)\subseteq[0,M),
 \qquad
 W_j\cap[0,M)\neq\varnothing
 \quad(j\neq i).
\end{equation}

Take
\[
 m>M,
 \qquad
 F\subseteq[M,m)\setminus W_i,
\]
and let
\begin{equation}\label{eq17}
 n_F
 =a+
 \sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\notin W_i}}2^t
 +\sum_{t\in F}2^t.
\end{equation}
By
\[
 {S}(a)\subseteq W_i,
 \qquad
 F\subseteq[M,m)\setminus W_i,
\]
and ${S}(a)\subseteq[0,M)$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 {S}(n_F)
 &={S}(a)
 \sqcup
 \bigl(([0,M)\cap\mathbb Z)\setminus W_i\bigr)
 \sqcup F,\\
 {S}(n_F)\cap W_i
 &={S}(a),\\
 0&<n_F<2^m.
\end{align*}

For $j\neq i$, let
\[
 b_j=P_j(M)+\sum_{t\in F\cap W_j}2^t.
\]
By
\[
 P_j(M)=\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\in W_j}}2^t,
 \qquad
 W_j\cap[0,M)\neq\varnothing,
\]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 {S}(b_j)
 &=\bigl(W_j\cap[0,M)\bigr)\sqcup(F\cap W_j)
 \subseteq W_j,\\
 {S}(b_j)&\neq\varnothing,
\end{align*}
and hence
\[
 b_j\in A_j\qquad(j\neq i).
\]
Moreover, since
\[
 ([0,M)\cap\mathbb Z)\setminus W_i
 =\bigsqcup_{j\neq i}(W_j\cap[0,M)),
\]
and
\[
 F=\bigsqcup_{j\neq i}(F\cap W_j),
\]
we have
\begin{align}
 n_F
 &=a+\sum_{j\neq i}
 \left(P_j(M)+\sum_{t\in F\cap W_j}2^t\right)
 \nonumber\\
 &=a+\sum_{j\neq i}b_j
 \in hA.
 \label{eq18}
\end{align}

Consider any representation with $h$ summands
\[
 n_F=c_1+\cdots+c_h,
 \qquad
 c_r\in A.
\]
For $1\leq j\leq h$, let
\(k_j=\left|\{r:c_r\in A_j\}\right|\).
Then
\begin{align*}
 k_j&\geq0,\\
 \sum_{j=1}^hk_j&=h,
\end{align*}
that is,
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathcal K_h.
\]
Let
\[
 N_M=2^w+\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\notin W_i}}2^t.
\]
By $w\in{S}(a)$ and the decomposition of ${S}(n_F)$ above,
\[
 {S}(N_M)
 =\{w\}\sqcup
 \bigl(([0,M)\cap\mathbb Z)\setminus W_i\bigr)
 \subseteq{S}(n_F).
\]
For each $r$, let $j_r$ be the unique index with
$c_r\in A_{j_r}\subseteq B_{j_r}$. Since
$S(N_M)\subseteq S(n_F)$, Lemma~\ref{lema3} gives
\[
 N_M=\sum_{r=1}^hc'_r,\qquad
 c'_r\in B_{j_r},\qquad
 S(c'_r)\subseteq S(c_r).
\]
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq19}
 N_M\in\sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j.
\end{equation}
This contradicts \eqref{eq15} when
$(k_1,\ldots,k_h)\neq(1,\ldots,1)$. Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq20}
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)=(1,\ldots,1).
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq20}, after relabeling the above representation we may write
\[
 n_F=c^{(1)}+\cdots+c^{(h)},
 \qquad
 c^{(j)}\in A_j.
\]
Then
\[
 {S}(c^{(j)})\subseteq W_j
 \qquad(1\leq j\leq h).
\]
From
\[
 W_r\cap W_s=\varnothing\qquad(r\neq s),
\]
we obtain
\[
 {S}(c^{(r)})\cap{S}(c^{(s)})=\varnothing
 \qquad(r\neq s).
\]
Since each binary position occurs in at most one summand, their sum involves no binary carries. Uniqueness of binary representations now gives
\begin{align*}
 S(n_F)&=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^h S(c^{(j)}),\\
 S(c^{(i)})&=S(n_F)\cap W_i=S(a),\\
 c^{(i)}&=\sum_{t\in S(c^{(i)})}2^t
 =\sum_{t\in S(a)}2^t=a.
\end{align*}
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq21}
 c^{(i)}=a.
\end{equation}
Hence every representation
\[
 n_F=c_1+\cdots+c_h,
 \qquad c_r\in A,
\]
satisfies
\[
 a\in\{c_1,\ldots,c_h\}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq18}, we obtain
\[
 n_F\in hA,
 \qquad
 n_F\notin h(A\setminus\{a\}),
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq22}
 n_F\in E_a.
\end{equation}

If
\(F_1\neq F_2\),
then by \eqref{eq17},
\[
 {S}(n_{F_1})\cap[M,m)=F_1
 \neq
 F_2={S}(n_{F_2})\cap[M,m).
\]
Thus $n_{F_1}\neq n_{F_2}$.
Moreover,
\begin{align}
 \left|[M,m)\setminus W_i\right|
 &=(m-M)-\left|W_i\cap[M,m)\right|
 \nonumber\\
 &=(m-M)-\bigl(W_i(m)-W_i(M)\bigr)
 \nonumber\\
 &=m-W_i(m)-M+W_i(M).
 \label{eq23}
\end{align}
Therefore, by \eqref{eq22},
\begin{align}
 E_a(2^m-1)
 &\geq
 \left|\{F:F\subseteq[M,m)\setminus W_i\}\right|
 \nonumber\\
 &=2^{\left|[M,m)\setminus W_i\right|}
 \nonumber\\
 &=2^{m-W_i(m)-M+W_i(M)}
 \nonumber\\
 &=2^{-M+W_i(M)}2^{m-W_i(m)}.
 \label{eq24}
\end{align}
By \eqref{eq14},
\begin{align}
 W_i(m)&=\frac mh+O(1),\nonumber\\
 m-W_i(m)&=\frac{h-1}{h}m+O(1).
 \label{eq25}
\end{align}
Substituting \eqref{eq25} into \eqref{eq24}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq26}
 E_a(2^m-1)\gg_a2^{(h-1)m/h}.
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq5} and \eqref{eq14},
\begin{align*}
 A(2^m-1)
 &=\sum_{j=1}^h\bigl(2^{W_j(m)}-1\bigr)\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^h2^{m/h+O(1)}-h\\
 &\asymp2^{m/h},
\end{align*}
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq27}
 A(2^m-1)\asymp2^{m/h}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq26} and \eqref{eq27},
\begin{align}
 E_a(2^m-1)
 &\gg_a2^{(h-1)m/h}
 \nonumber\\
 &\asymp A(2^m-1)^{h-1},
 \label{eq28}
\end{align}
and hence
\[
 E_a(2^m-1)\gg_a A(2^m-1)^{h-1}.
\]

For sufficiently large $x$, choose an integer $m$ such that
\(2^m\leq x+1<2^{m+1}\).
Then
\(2^m-1\leq x<2^{m+1}-1\).
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 E_a(x)
 &\geq E_a(2^m-1)\\
 &\gg_a2^{(h-1)m/h},
\end{align*}
and
\begin{align*}
 A(x)
 &\leq A(2^{m+1}-1)\\
 &\ll2^{(m+1)/h},
\end{align*}
Hence
\begin{align*}
 A(x)^{h-1}
 &\ll2^{(h-1)(m+1)/h}\\
 &=2^{(h-1)/h}2^{(h-1)m/h}\\
 &\ll_a E_a(x).
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
 E_a(x)\gg_a A(x)^{h-1}.
\]
Since
\(a\in A\)
was arbitrary, $A$ is a strongly minimal asymptotic basis of order $h$.
head: environment
name: Proof of sufficiency

label: lema6
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an integer $L_a$ such that
\[
 {S}(a)\subseteq[0,L_a),
 \qquad
 a<2^{L_a}.
\]
Fix a sufficiently large integer $m>L_a$ and $n\in E_a\cap[0,2^m)$.
Since
\(E_a\subseteq hA\),
we may choose a representation
\[
 n=a_1+\cdots+a_h,
 \qquad
 a_r\in A\quad(1\leq r\leq h).
\]
Moreover, since
\(n\notin h(A\setminus\{a\})\),
at least one summand in this representation is equal to $a$. Let
\(R=\{r\in\{1,\ldots,h\}:a_r=a\}\).
Then
\(1\leq\left|R\right|\leq h\).

We first prove that if $s\notin R$ and $a_s\in A_i$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq30}
 \left|\bigl({S}(a_s)\cap[L_a,m)\bigr)\right|\leq h-1.
\end{equation}
Suppose, for a contradiction, that
\[
 \left|\bigl({S}(a_s)\cap[L_a,m)\bigr)\right|\geq h.
\]
Since $s\notin R$,
\(\left|R\right|\leq h-1\).
Therefore, for every $r\in R$, we may choose distinct integers
\[
 v_r\in{S}(a_s)\cap[L_a,m).
\]
Since
\(a_s\in A_i\),
we obtain
\[
 {S}(a_s)\subseteq W_i,
 \qquad
 v_r\in W_i.
\]
Moreover, since
\[
 {S}(a)\subseteq[0,L_a),
 \qquad
 v_r\geq L_a,
\]
we have
\(v_r\notin{S}(a)\).
For $r\in R$, define
\(a'_r=a+2^{v_r}\).
Then
\[
 {S}(a'_r)={S}(a)\sqcup\{v_r\}\subseteq W_i,
\]
and hence
\[
 a'_r\in A_i,
 \qquad
 a'_r\neq a.
\]
Next define
\(a'_s=a_s-\sum_{r\in R}2^{v_r}\).
Since the $v_r$ are distinct elements of $S(a_s)$,
\[
 S(a'_s)=S(a_s)\setminus\{v_r:r\in R\},
\]
so that
\begin{align*}
 \left|\bigl({S}(a'_s)\cap[L_a,m)\bigr)\right|
 &\geq
 \left|\bigl({S}(a_s)\cap[L_a,m)\bigr)\right|-\left|R\right|\\
 &\geq h-(h-1)\\
 &=1.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
 a'_s>0,
 \qquad
 {S}(a'_s)\subseteq W_i,
\]
and hence
\(a'_s\in A_i\).
Since $S(a'_s)\cap[L_a,m)\neq\varnothing$ whereas
$S(a)\cap[L_a,m)=\varnothing$, we also have $a'_s\neq a$.
For the remaining indices, define
\[
 a'_r=a_r
 \qquad(r\notin R\cup\{s\}).
\]
Since these indices are not in $R$,
\[
 a'_r=a_r\in A\setminus\{a\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 a'_r\in A\setminus\{a\}
 \qquad(1\leq r\leq h).
\]
On the other hand,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{r=1}^{h}a'_r
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{h}a_r
   +\sum_{r\in R}2^{v_r}
   -\sum_{r\in R}2^{v_r}\\
 &=n.
\end{align*}
Thus $n\in h(A\setminus\{a\})$, contrary to $n\in E_a$.
This proves \eqref{eq30}. The same bound holds trivially for $a_r=a$, since
$S(a)\cap[L_a,m)=\varnothing$.

We estimate the number of elements of $A_i$ satisfying \eqref{eq30}. If
\(b\in A_i, \qquad 0<b<2^m\),
then
\({S}(b)\subseteq W_i\cap[0,m)\).
The choices for the two disjoint ranges satisfy
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \#\{U:U\subseteq W_i\cap[0,L_a)\}&=2^{W_i(L_a)},\\
 \#\{U\subseteq W_i\cap[L_a,m):|U|\leq h-1\}
 &\leq\sum_{r=0}^{h-1}\binom{W_i(m)-W_i(L_a)}r.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq31}
\begin{aligned}
&\left|\{b\in A_i:0<b<2^m,\ \left|S(b)\cap[L_a,m)\right|\leq h-1\}\right|\\
&\quad\leq 2^{W_i(L_a)}
\sum_{r=0}^{h-1}\binom{W_i(m)-W_i(L_a)}{r}\\
&\quad\leq 2^{W_i(L_a)}
\sum_{r=0}^{h-1}\binom{m-L_a}{r}\\
&\quad\leq C_{a,h}(m+1)^{h-1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq5},
\begin{equation}\label{eq32}
\begin{aligned}
A(2^m-1)
&=\sum_{j=1}^{h}\bigl(2^{W_j(m)}-1\bigr)\\
&\leq\sum_{j=1}^{h}2^{W_j(m)}
\leq h2^{K(m)}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Fix
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 0\leq n<2^m,\qquad n\in E_a,\qquad
 {S}(n)\cap W_i\neq{S}(a),\\
 n=\sum_{u=1}^{h}a_u,\qquad a_u\in A\ (1\leq u\leq h),
 \qquad a_{s_0}=a.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Let $N_1(m)$ and $N_2(m)$ denote the numbers of integers $n$
admitting representations of the following two types, respectively.

\noindent\emph{\bf Case 1.} Suppose that, for some $1\leq r\leq h-1$,
\[
 \left|\{u\neq s_0:a_u\in A_i\}\right|=r.
\]
By \eqref{eq30}, \eqref{eq31}, and
\eqref{eq32},
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left|\{b\in A_i:0<b<2^m,\
 \ \left|{S}(b)\cap[L_a,m)\right|\leq h-1\}\right|
 \leq C_{a,h}(m+1)^{h-1},\\
 &\left|\{b\in A:0<b<2^m\}\right|
 =A(2^m-1)\leq h2^{K(m)},\\
 \end{aligned}
\]
The positions of $a$ and the $r$ remaining $A_i$-summands
admit at most $h\binom{h-1}{r}$ choices. Hence
\begin{align}
 N_1(m)
 &\leq h\sum_{r=1}^{h-1}\binom{h-1}{r}
 \bigl(C_{a,h}(m+1)^{h-1}\bigr)^r
 \bigl(h2^{K(m)}\bigr)^{h-1-r}
 \nonumber\\
 &\leq C'_{a,h}\sum_{r=1}^{h-1}
 (m+1)^{r(h-1)}2^{(h-1-r)K(m)}
 \nonumber\\
 &\leq C''_{a,h}(m+1)^{(h-1)^2}2^{(h-2)K(m)}.
 \label{eq33}
\end{align}
Since $K(m)\geq m/h$,
\begin{align}
 \frac{N_1(m)}{2^{(h-1)K(m)}}
 &\leq C''_{a,h}(m+1)^{(h-1)^2}2^{-K(m)}
 \nonumber\\
 &\leq C''_{a,h}(m+1)^{(h-1)^2}2^{-m/h}
 \longrightarrow0.
 \label{eq34}
\end{align}
Thus
\[
 N_1(m)=o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr).
\]

\noindent\emph{\bf Case 2.} Suppose that
\[
 a_u\notin A_i\qquad(u\neq s_0).
\]
For $j\neq i$, put
\[
 r_j=\left|\{u\neq s_0:a_u\in A_j\}\right|,\qquad
 r_j\geq0,\qquad\sum_{j\neq i}r_j=h-1.
\]
If $(r_j)_{j\neq i}=(1,\ldots,1)$, let $b_j\in A_j$ be
the unique $A_j$-summand for $j\neq i$. Since their binary
supports are disjoint,
\[
 n=a+\sum_{j\neq i}b_j,
 \qquad
 S(n)\cap W_i=S(a),
\]
contrary to the choice of $n$. Hence
$(r_j)_{j\neq i}\neq(1,\ldots,1)$, and, since
$\sum_{j\neq i}r_j=h-1$, we have
\[
 \max_{j\neq i}r_j\geq2.
\]

Fix such a vector $(r_j)_{j\neq i}$ and write its summands as
$a_{j,1},\ldots,a_{j,r_j}\in A_j$. Since
$0<a_{j,u}\leq n<2^m$, for $j\neq i$ we have
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{u=1}^{r_j}a_{j,u}
 &=\sum_{t\in W_j\cap[0,m)}
 \left(\sum_{u=1}^{r_j}\varepsilon_t(a_{j,u})\right)2^t,\\
 0&\leq\sum_{u=1}^{r_j}\varepsilon_t(a_{j,u})\leq r_j
 \qquad(t\in W_j\cap[0,m)).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq35}
\begin{aligned}
N_2(m;(r_j)_{j\ne i})
&\leq \prod_{j\ne i}(r_j+1)^{W_j(m)}\\
&\leq \prod_{j\ne i}(r_j+1)^{K(m)}\\
&=2^{K(m)\sum_{j\ne i}\log_2(r_j+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \log_2(r+1)&=r &&(r=0,1),\\
 r+1&\leq3\cdot2^{r-2} &&(r\geq2),\\
 \log_2(r+1)&\leq r-2+\log_2 3 &&(r\geq2).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq36}
 \delta=2-\log_2 3>0.
\end{equation}
Since $\max_{j\neq i}r_j\geq2$,
\[
 \sum_{j\neq i}\log_2(r_j+1)
 \leq\sum_{j\neq i}r_j-\delta
 =h-1-\delta.
\]
Thus
\[
 N_2(m;(r_j)_{j\neq i})
 \leq2^{(h-1-\delta)K(m)}.
\]
The number of possible vectors satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\#\left\{(r_j)_{j\ne i}\in\mathbb N_0^{h-1}:
\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{j\ne i}r_j=h-1,\\[-1pt]
\max_{j\ne i}r_j\geq2
\end{array}\right\}\\
&\qquad=\binom{2h-3}{h-2}-1
\leq\binom{2h-3}{h-2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq37}
\begin{aligned}
N_2(m)
&\leq\binom{2h-3}{h-2}2^{(h-1-\delta)K(m)}\\
&=O_h\bigl(2^{(h-1-\delta)K(m)}\bigr)\\
&=o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Every integer under consideration occurs in at least one of the two cases. The cases need not be disjoint, so possible multiple representations only strengthen the following upper bound. Thus, by \eqref{eq34} and \eqref{eq37},
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|\{0\leq n<2^m:n\in E_a,\ S(n)\cap W_i\ne S(a)\}\right|\\
&\quad\leq N_1(m)+N_2(m)
=o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is \eqref{eq29}.
head: environment

label: lema7
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lema7} If $A$ is a strongly minimal asymptotic basis of order $h$, then there exists a constant $C>0$ such that
\[
 \left|W_i(m)-\frac mh\right|\leq C
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq h,\ m\geq0).
\]
head: environment

label: eq38
title: Proof
body_md:
Since each $W_i$ is infinite, each $A_i$ is infinite. For
$1\leq i\leq h$, fix
\(a_i\in A_i\).
By strong minimality, for each $i$ there exist a constant $c_i>0$ and an integer $m_i$ such that, for
$m\geq m_i$,
\[
 E_{a_i}(2^m-1)
 \geq
 c_iA(2^m-1)^{h-1}.
\]
By \eqref{eq5},
\[
 A(2^m-1)
 =\sum_{j=1}^{h}\bigl(2^{W_j(m)}-1\bigr).
\]
Choose $j_0$ such that $W_{j_0}(m)=K(m)$. Then
\begin{align*}
 K(m)&\geq\frac1h\sum_{j=1}^hW_j(m)=\frac mh\longrightarrow\infty,\\
 A(2^m-1)&=\sum_{j=1}^h(2^{W_j(m)}-1)
 \geq 2^{K(m)}-1\geq2^{K(m)-1}
\end{align*}
for all sufficiently large $m$.
Hence, for every $i$, there exists a constant $c'_i>0$ such that
\begin{align}
 E_{a_i}(2^m-1)
 &\geq c_iA(2^m-1)^{h-1}
 \nonumber\\
 &\geq c_i\bigl(2^{K(m)-1}\bigr)^{h-1}
 \nonumber\\
 &=c'_i2^{(h-1)K(m)}
 \label{eq38}
\end{align}
for all sufficiently large $m$.

Fix $m$ with $S(a_i)\subseteq[0,m)$. Partition the elements of
$E_{a_i}\cap[0,2^m)$ according to whether $S(n)\cap W_i=S(a_i)$.
In the first class,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\varepsilon_t(n)=
\begin{cases}
1,&t\in S(a_i),\\
0,&t\in(W_i\cap[0,m))\setminus S(a_i),
\end{cases}\\[2pt]
\#\bigl(([0,m)\cap\mathbb Z)\setminus W_i\bigr)=m-W_i(m).
\end{gathered}
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \#\{0\leq n<2^m:S(n)\cap W_i=S(a_i)\}
 &=2^{m-W_i(m)},\\
 \#\{0\leq n<2^m:n\in E_{a_i},\ S(n)\cap W_i\neq S(a_i)\}
 &=o(2^{(h-1)K(m)})
\end{align*}
by Lemma~\ref{lema6}. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq39}
 E_{a_i}(2^m-1)
 \leq
 2^{m-W_i(m)}
 +o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr).
\end{equation}

Combining \eqref{eq38} and \eqref{eq39}, for each fixed $i$ we have
\[
 c'_i2^{(h-1)K(m)}
 \leq
 2^{m-W_i(m)}
 +o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr).
\]
For sufficiently large $m$,
\[
 o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr)
 \leq
 \frac{c'_i}{2}2^{(h-1)K(m)}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 2^{m-W_i(m)}
 \geq
 \frac{c'_i}{2}2^{(h-1)K(m)}.
\]
Since there are only finitely many indices $i$, we may choose a positive constant $c$, depending only on the $c'_i$, such that for every $i$ and all sufficiently large $m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq40}
 2^{m-W_i(m)}
 \geq
 c\,2^{(h-1)K(m)}.
\end{equation}

Choose $i(m)$ with $W_{i(m)}(m)=K(m)$. Since the constant
$c$ in \eqref{eq40} is independent of $i$,
\begin{align*}
 2^{m-K(m)}&\geq c\,2^{(h-1)K(m)},
 \end{align*}
and so
\[ hK(m)\leq m-\log_2c.\]

Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq41}
 K(m)\leq\frac mh+C_1
\end{equation}
for some constant $C_1>0$ and all sufficiently large $m$.

Since $W_i(m)\leq K(m)$,
\[
 W_i(m)\leq\frac mh+C_1
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq h).
\]
By \eqref{eq2},
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{h}W_j(m)=m.
\]
Fix $i$. Then
\begin{align*}
 W_i(m)
 &=m-\sum_{j\neq i}W_j(m)\\
 &\geq
 m-\sum_{j\neq i}\left(\frac mh+C_1\right)\\
 &=m-(h-1)\frac mh-(h-1)C_1\\
 &=\frac mh-(h-1)C_1.
\end{align*}
Therefore, for all sufficiently large $m$,
\[
 \frac mh-(h-1)C_1
 \leq
 W_i(m)
 \leq
 \frac mh+C_1.
\]
Hence there exists a constant $C_2>0$ such that
\[
 \left|W_i(m)-\frac mh\right|\leq C_2
\]
for all $1\leq i\leq h$ and all sufficiently large $m$. Increasing the constant to cover the finitely many smaller values of $m$, we obtain $C>0$ such that
\[
 \left|W_i(m)-\frac mh\right|\leq C
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq h,\ m\geq0).
\]
This completes the proof of the lemma.
head: environment

label: lema8
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lema8} Let $a\in A_i$, let $I=[s,s+L)\cap\mathbb Z$, and suppose that
\(s>\max S(a)\).
Let $\mathcal P$ be an index set with $\left|\mathcal P\right|=h$, and suppose that
\[
 b_p\in A\cup\{0\}\qquad(p\in\mathcal P).
\]
Suppose that there exist $p_*\in\mathcal P$ and $\ell\in\{1,\ldots,h\}$ such that
\[
 b:=b_{p_*}\in A_\ell,
 \qquad
 \left|{S}(b)\cap I\right|\geq h.
\]
Put
\[
 R=\{p\in\mathcal P:b_p=a\},
 \qquad
 Z=\{p\in\mathcal P:b_p=0\}.
\]
If
\[
 R=\varnothing
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 \ell=i,
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b_p\in h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S(b)\cap I\neq\varnothing$ whereas
$S(a)\cap I=\varnothing$, we have $b>0$ and $b\neq a$. Thus
\[
 p_*\notin R\cup Z,\qquad
 |R|+|Z|=|R\cup Z|\leq|\mathcal P|-1=h-1.
\]

By
\[
 \left|{S}(b)\cap I\right|\geq h
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \left|R\cup Z\right|\leq h-1,
\]
we may choose, for every $p\in R\cup Z$, distinct integers
\(v_p\in{S}(b)\cap I\).
Let
\(V=\{v_p:p\in R\cup Z\}\).
Then
\[
 V\subseteq{S}(b)\cap I,
 \qquad
 \left|V\right|=\left|R\right|+\left|Z\right|\leq h-1.
\]
Define
\[
 b'_p=
 \begin{cases}
 a+2^{v_p},&p\in R,\\
 2^{v_p},&p\in Z,\\
 b-\displaystyle\sum_{v\in V}2^v,&p=p_*,\\
 b_p,&p\in\mathcal P\setminus(R\cup Z\cup\{p_*\}).
 \end{cases}
\]
We show that
\[
 b'_p\in A\setminus\{a\}.
\]

If $p\in R$, then $R\neq\varnothing$. By hypothesis,
\[
 R=\varnothing
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 \ell=i,
\]
we must have
\(\ell=i\).
Therefore,
\[
 v_p\in{S}(b)\subseteq W_i.
\]
Moreover, since
\(v_p\in I, \qquad s>\max S(a)\),
we have
\[
 v_p>\max S(a),
 \qquad
 v_p\notin{S}(a).
\]
Hence
\[
 {S}(b'_p)
 ={S}(a+2^{v_p})
 ={S}(a)\sqcup\{v_p\}
 \subseteq W_i.
\]
Consequently,
\(b'_p\in A_i\).
Furthermore,
\(b'_p=a+2^{v_p}>a\),
so
\[
 b'_p\in A_i\setminus\{a\}.
\]

For $p\in Z$, we have
\(v_p\in{S}(b)\subseteq W_\ell\),
and hence
\({S}(b'_p)=\{v_p\}\subseteq W_\ell\).
Therefore,
\[
 b'_p=2^{v_p}\in A_\ell.
\]
Since $v_p\in I$ and $S(a)\cap I=\varnothing$, we also have
$b'_p\neq a$. Thus $b'_p\in A\setminus\{a\}$.

For $p=p_*$, since
\(V\subseteq{S}(b)\),
we have
\[
 b'_{p_*}
 =b-\sum_{v\in V}2^v
 =\sum_{t\in{S}(b)\setminus V}2^t.
\]
Furthermore,
\begin{align*}
 \left|({S}(b)\cap I)\setminus V\right|
 &\geq
 \left|{S}(b)\cap I\right|-\left|V\right|\\
 &\geq h-(h-1)\\
 &=1.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
 {S}(b)\setminus V\neq\varnothing,
 \qquad
 b'_{p_*}>0.
\]
Also,
\[
 {S}(b'_{p_*})={S}(b)\setminus V\subseteq W_\ell,
\]
and hence
\(b'_{p_*}\in A_\ell\).
Moreover, $S(b'_{p_*})\cap I\neq\varnothing$ whereas
$S(a)\cap I=\varnothing$. Thus $b'_{p_*}\in A\setminus\{a\}$.

Finally, take
\[
 p\in\mathcal P\setminus(R\cup Z\cup\{p_*\}).
\]
Since $p\notin Z$,
\(b_p\neq0\).
Using also
\(b_p\in A\cup\{0\}\),
we obtain
\(b_p\in A\).
Moreover, since $p\notin R$,
\(b_p\neq a\).
Therefore,
\[
 b'_p=b_p\in A\setminus\{a\}.
\]
Consequently, for every $p\in\mathcal P$,
\[
 b'_p\in A\setminus\{a\}.
\]

It remains to check the sum. Since $V=\{v_p:p\in R\cup Z\}$ and the $v_p$ are distinct,
\[
 \sum_{v\in V}2^v
 =\sum_{p\in R}2^{v_p}+\sum_{p\in Z}2^{v_p}.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b'_p
 &=\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b_p
   +\sum_{p\in R}2^{v_p}
   +\sum_{p\in Z}2^{v_p}
   -\sum_{v\in V}2^v\\
 &=\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b_p.
\end{align*}
Hence
\[
 \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b_p
 =\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}b'_p
 \in h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\]
This completes the proof of the lemma.
head: environment

label: lema9
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lema9} Suppose that, for some constant $C>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq42}
 \left|W_j(m)-\frac mh\right|\leq C
 \qquad(1\leq j\leq h,\ m\geq0).
\end{equation}
Then there exists an integer $L=L(h,C)\geq1$ with the following property. For every $i\in\{1,\ldots,h\}$, every $a\in A_i$, every interval $I=[s,s+L)\cap\mathbb Z$ with $s>\max S(a)$, and every
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\},
\]
if an integer $n$ has binary digits $0$ at all positions in $W_i\cap I$ and binary digits $1$ at all positions in $I\setminus W_i$, then
\[
 n\in\sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 n\in h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\]
head: environment

label: eq43
title: Proof
body_md:
For every interval $I=[s,s+L)\cap\mathbb Z$, where $s\geq0$ and $L\geq1$ are integers, put $m_j(I)=\left|W_j\cap I\right|$. By \eqref{eq42},
\begin{align}
 m_j(I)
 &=W_j(s+L)-W_j(s)
 \nonumber\\
 &=\frac Lh+e_j,
 \qquad
 |e_j|\leq2C.
 \label{eq43}
\end{align}
Let $D=2C$ and choose the integer
\begin{equation}\label{eq44}
 L=
 \left\lfloor
 \max\left\{
 h\bigl((2h+1)D+2(h-1)\bigr),
 h\bigl(2hD+h^2-1\bigr),
 \frac{hD}{h-1}+h(h+1)
 \right\}
 \right\rfloor+1.
\end{equation}
By this choice,
\begin{equation}\label{eq45}
 \frac Lh-D>2hD+2(h-1),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq46}
 \frac Lh-2hD-(h-1)>h(h-1),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq47}
 \frac{h-1}{h}L-D-(h-1)>h(h-1).
\end{equation}

Let
\[
 I=[s,s+L)\cap\mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 s>\max S(a),
\]
and suppose that
\[
 n\in\sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j,
 \qquad
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\}.
\]
Since
\(\sum_{j=1}^hk_j=h\),
we may choose
\[
 b_{j,r}\in B_j
 \qquad
 (1\leq j\leq h,\ 1\leq r\leq k_j)
\]
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq48}
 n=\sum_{j=1}^h\sum_{r=1}^{k_j}b_{j,r}.
\end{equation}
The summands $b_{j,r}$ may be $0$. Let
\[
 \mathcal P=
 \{(j,r):1\leq j\leq h,\ 1\leq r\leq k_j\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq49}
 \left|\mathcal P\right|=\sum_{j=1}^hk_j=h.
\end{equation}

For $(j,r)\in\mathcal P$, since
\(b_{j,r}\in B_j=A(W_j)\cup\{0\}\)
we may write
\[
 b_{j,r}=\sum_{u\geq0}\varepsilon_u(b_{j,r})2^u,
\]
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq50}
 \varepsilon_u(b_{j,r})\in\{0,1\},
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_u(b_{j,r})=0\quad(u\notin W_j).
\end{equation}
Since
\(\mathbb N_0=W_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup W_h\),
for every $t\geq0$ there exists a unique
\[
 c(t)\in\{1,\ldots,h\}
\]
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq51}
 t\in W_{c(t)}.
\end{equation}
Let
\begin{align}
 d_t
 &:=\sum_{j=1}^h\sum_{r=1}^{k_j}\varepsilon_t(b_{j,r})
 \nonumber\\
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{k_{c(t)}}\varepsilon_t(b_{c(t),r}).
 \label{eq52}
\end{align}
Then
\begin{align}
 0\leq d_t
 &\leq\sum_{r=1}^{k_{c(t)}}1
 =k_{c(t)}
 \leq\sum_{j=1}^hk_j
 =h.
 \label{eq53}
\end{align}
By \eqref{eq48},
\begin{align}
 n
 &=\sum_{j=1}^h\sum_{r=1}^{k_j}
   \sum_{u\geq0}\varepsilon_u(b_{j,r})2^u
 \nonumber\\
 &=\sum_{u\geq0}
   \left(\sum_{j=1}^h\sum_{r=1}^{k_j}\varepsilon_u(b_{j,r})\right)2^u
 \nonumber\\
 &=\sum_{u\geq0}d_u2^u.
 \label{eq54}
\end{align}
On the other hand, with the notation above, the standard binary expansion of $n$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq55}
 n=\sum_{u\geq0}\varepsilon_u(n)2^u,
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_u(n)\in\{0,1\}.
\end{equation}
By the hypothesis of the lemma, for $t\in I$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq56}
 \varepsilon_t(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&t\in W_i\cap I,\\
 1,&t\in I\setminus W_i.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}

We now compare \eqref{eq54} and
\eqref{eq55} by binary carries. Put $c_0=0$ and, for
$t\geq0$, let
\[
 S_t=\sum_{u=0}^{t}d_u2^u,
 \qquad
 T_t=\sum_{u=0}^{t}\varepsilon_u(n)2^u.
\]
Both expansions represent $n$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq57}
 S_t\equiv n\pmod{2^{t+1}},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq58}
 T_t\equiv n\pmod{2^{t+1}}.
\end{equation}
Since
\[
 S_t\geq0,
 \qquad
 0\leq T_t\leq2^{t+1}-1,
 \qquad
 S_t\equiv T_t\pmod{2^{t+1}},
\]
there exists a unique integer $c_{t+1}\geq0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq59}
 \sum_{u=0}^{t}d_u2^u
 =
 \sum_{u=0}^{t}\varepsilon_u(n)2^u
 +2^{t+1}c_{t+1}.
\end{equation}
For $t\geq1$, substituting $t-1$ into
\eqref{eq59} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq60}
 \sum_{u=0}^{t-1}d_u2^u
 =
 \sum_{u=0}^{t-1}\varepsilon_u(n)2^u
 +2^tc_t.
\end{equation}
Subtracting the two equalities,
\[
 d_t2^t
 =\varepsilon_t(n)2^t+2^{t+1}c_{t+1}-2^tc_t,
\]
and hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq61}
 d_t+c_t=\varepsilon_t(n)+2c_{t+1}
 \qquad(t\geq1).
\end{equation}
For $t=0$, the same identity follows from
\eqref{eq59} and $c_0=0$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq62}
 d_t+c_t=\varepsilon_t(n)+2c_{t+1}
 \qquad(t\geq0).
\end{equation}

We next prove that the carries are uniformly bounded. We already have
\(c_0=0\leq h-1\).
If
\(0\leq c_t\leq h-1\),
then, by \eqref{eq62} and \eqref{eq53},
\begin{align*}
 0\leq2c_{t+1}
 &=d_t+c_t-\varepsilon_t(n)\\
 &\leq d_t+c_t\\
 &\leq h+(h-1)=2h-1.
\end{align*}
Since $c_{t+1}$ is an integer,
\[
 0\leq c_{t+1}
 \leq\left\lfloor\frac{2h-1}{2}\right\rfloor
 =h-1.
\]
By induction,
\begin{equation}\label{eq63}
\begin{gathered}
d_t+c_t=\varepsilon_t(n)+2c_{t+1},\\[2pt]
0\leq d_t\leq k_{c(t)},\qquad
0\leq c_t\leq h-1
\qquad(t\geq0).
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

Summing
\eqref{eq63} over $t=s,\ldots,s+L-1$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}d_t
 +\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}c_t
 &=\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}\varepsilon_t(n)
 +2\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}c_{t+1}\\
 &=\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}\varepsilon_t(n)
 +2\sum_{t=s+1}^{s+L}c_t\\
 &=\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}\varepsilon_t(n)
 +2\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}c_t
 -2c_s+2c_{s+L}.
\end{align*}
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq64}
 \sum_{t\in I}c_t
 =\sum_{t\in I}(d_t-\varepsilon_t(n))
 +2c_s-2c_{s+L}.
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq63} and $0\leq c_t\leq h-1$, we have
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\in I}(d_t-\varepsilon_t(n))
 &=\sum_{t=s}^{s+L-1}(2c_{t+1}-c_t)\\
 &=\sum_{t=s+1}^{s+L-1}c_t+2c_{s+L}-c_s\\
 &\geq-c_s\\
 &\geq-(h-1).
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq72}
 \sum_{t\in I}d_t
 \geq\sum_{t\in I}\varepsilon_t(n)-(h-1).
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq56},
\begin{equation}\label{eq73}
 \sum_{t\in I}\varepsilon_t(n)
 =\sum_{j\neq i}m_j(I).
\end{equation}

We distinguish three cases according to $k_i$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 1. $k_i=1$.} For $t\in W_i\cap I$, by \eqref{eq56} and
\eqref{eq53},
\[
 \varepsilon_t(n)=0,
 \qquad
 d_t\in\{0,1\}.
\]
By \eqref{eq63},
$d_t+c_t=2c_{t+1}$. If $d_t=0$, then $d_t\leq c_t$.
If $d_t=1$, then $c_t=2c_{t+1}-1\geq1=d_t$.
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq74}
 d_t\leq c_t
 \qquad(t\in W_i\cap I).
\end{equation}

By \eqref{eq64},
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}c_t
 +\sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}c_t\\
 &=\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}d_t
 +\sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}d_t
 -\sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}1
 +2c_s-2c_{s+L}.
\end{align*}
For $j\neq i$ and $t\in W_j\cap I$,
\(d_t\leq k_j\),
Hence
\[
 \sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}d_t
 =\sum_{j\neq i}\sum_{t\in W_j\cap I}d_t
 \leq\sum_{j\neq i}k_jm_j(I).
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}1
 =\sum_{j\neq i}m_j(I),
\]
and
\[
 -2c_{s+L}\leq0,
 \qquad
 2c_s\leq2(h-1).
\]
Combining these with \eqref{eq74} and cancelling
$\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}c_t$, we obtain
\begin{align}
 \sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}c_t
 &\leq
 \sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)m_j(I)+2(h-1).
 \label{eq75}
\end{align}
Since $k_i=1$ and $\sum_{j=1}^hk_j=h$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq76}
 \sum_{j\neq i}k_j=h-1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)=0.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq43}, write
\[
 m_j(I)=\frac Lh+e_j,
 \qquad |e_j|\leq D.
\]
Then \eqref{eq76} gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)m_j(I)
 &=\frac Lh\sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)
 +\sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)e_j\\
 &=\sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)e_j\\
 &\leq D\sum_{j\neq i}|k_j-1|.
\end{align*}
Moreover, since
\[
 k_j\geq0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{j\neq i}k_j=h-1,
\]
we have
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j\neq i}|k_j-1|
 &\leq\sum_{j\neq i}(k_j+1)\\
 &=\sum_{j\neq i}k_j+(h-1)\\
 &=2(h-1)<2h.
\end{align*}
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq77}
 \sum_{j\neq i}(k_j-1)m_j(I)\leq2hD.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq75} and \eqref{eq77},
\begin{equation}\label{eq78}
 \sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}c_t
 \leq2hD+2(h-1).
\end{equation}

Since $k_i=1$, $\sum_{j\neq i}k_j=h-1$, but
$(k_1,\ldots,k_h)\neq(1,\ldots,1)$. Thus some index
$j_0\neq i$ satisfies $k_{j_0}=0$.
For $t\in W_{j_0}\cap I$, by
\eqref{eq53} and \eqref{eq56},
\[
 d_t=0,
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_t(n)=1.
\]
so \eqref{eq63} gives
\(c_t=1+2c_{t+1}\geq1\).
Therefore,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{t\in I\setminus W_i}c_t
 &\geq\sum_{t\in W_{j_0}\cap I}c_t
 \nonumber\\
 &\geq m_{j_0}(I)
 \nonumber\\
 &\geq\frac Lh-D.
 \label{eq79}
\end{align}
By \eqref{eq45},
\[
 \frac Lh-D>2hD+2(h-1).
\]
This contradicts \eqref{eq78} and \eqref{eq79}.
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq80}
 k_i\neq1.
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 2. $k_i\geq2$.} By \eqref{eq53},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\in I}d_t
 &=\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}d_t
 +\sum_{j\neq i}\sum_{t\in W_j\cap I}d_t\\
 &\leq\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}d_t
 +\sum_{j\neq i}k_jm_j(I).
\end{align*}
Therefore, by \eqref{eq72} and \eqref{eq73},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}d_t
 &\geq
 \sum_{j\neq i}m_j(I)-(h-1)
 -\sum_{j\neq i}k_jm_j(I)\\
 &=\sum_{j\neq i}(1-k_j)m_j(I)-(h-1).
\end{align*}
Moreover,
\[
 \sum_{j\neq i}(1-k_j)
 =(h-1)-(h-k_i)=k_i-1.
\]
Using
\[
 m_j(I)=\frac Lh+e_j,
 \qquad |e_j|\leq D,
\]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j\neq i}(1-k_j)m_j(I)
 &=\frac Lh(k_i-1)
 +\sum_{j\neq i}(1-k_j)e_j\\
 &\geq\frac Lh(k_i-1)
 -D\sum_{j\neq i}|1-k_j|.
\end{align*}
Also,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{j\neq i}|1-k_j|
 &\leq\sum_{j\neq i}(1+k_j)\\
 &=(h-1)+(h-k_i)\\
 &\leq2h.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}d_t
 &\geq
 (k_i-1)\frac Lh-2hD-(h-1)
 \nonumber\\
 &\geq
 \frac Lh-2hD-(h-1)
 \nonumber\\
 &>h(h-1),
 \label{eq81}
\end{align}
where the last step follows from \eqref{eq46}.

For $1\leq r\leq k_i$, let
\(q_r=\left|{S}(b_{i,r})\cap I\right|\).
By \eqref{eq52},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{r=1}^{k_i}q_r
 &=\sum_{r=1}^{k_i}\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}\varepsilon_t(b_{i,r})\\
 &=\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}\sum_{r=1}^{k_i}\varepsilon_t(b_{i,r})\\
 &=\sum_{t\in W_i\cap I}d_t\\
 &>h(h-1).
\end{align*}
Since $k_i\leq h$, the inequality above gives
$\sum_{r=1}^{k_i}q_r>k_i(h-1)$. Thus there exists
$r_*$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq82}
 b:=b_{i,r_*}\in A_i,
 \qquad
 \left|{S}(b)\cap I\right|\geq h.
\end{equation}
Let
\(p_*=(i,r_*)\).
By \eqref{eq48}, \eqref{eq49},
\eqref{eq82}, and Lemma~\ref{lema8} (with
$\ell=i$), we obtain
in the case $k_i\geq2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq83}
 n\in h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\end{equation}

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 3. $k_i=0$.} By \eqref{eq72} and \eqref{eq73},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{t\in I}d_t
 &\geq\sum_{j\neq i}m_j(I)-(h-1)\\
 &=L-m_i(I)-(h-1).
\end{align*}
By \eqref{eq43},
\[
 m_i(I)=\frac Lh+e_i,
 \qquad |e_i|\leq D,
\]
and hence
\begin{align}
 \sum_{t\in I}d_t
 &\geq L-\left(\frac Lh+D\right)-(h-1)
 \nonumber\\
 &=\frac{h-1}{h}L-D-(h-1)
 \nonumber\\
 &>h(h-1),
 \label{eq84}
\end{align}
where the last step follows from \eqref{eq47}.

For every $p=(j,r)\in\mathcal P$, let
\(q_p=\left|{S}(b_p)\cap I\right|\).
By \eqref{eq52},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}q_p
 &=\sum_{j=1}^h\sum_{r=1}^{k_j}
   \sum_{t\in I}\varepsilon_t(b_{j,r})\\
 &=\sum_{t\in I}
   \sum_{j=1}^h\sum_{r=1}^{k_j}\varepsilon_t(b_{j,r})\\
 &=\sum_{t\in I}d_t\\
 &>h(h-1).
\end{align*}
Since $|\mathcal P|=h$, the inequality above gives
$\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}q_p>|\mathcal P|(h-1)$. Thus
there exists $p_*=(j_*,r_*)\in\mathcal P$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq85}
 b:=b_{p_*}\in A_{j_*},
 \qquad
 \left|{S}(b)\cap I\right|\geq h.
\end{equation}
Since $k_i=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq86}
 j_*\neq i.
\end{equation}
For all $p=(j,r)\in\mathcal P$, we have $j\neq i$, and hence
\[
 b_p\in B_j=A_j\cup\{0\},\qquad
 (A_j\cup\{0\})\cap A_i=\varnothing,
 \qquad a\in A_i.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq87}
 \{p\in\mathcal P:b_p=a\}=\varnothing.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq48}, \eqref{eq49},
\eqref{eq85}--\eqref{eq87}, and
Lemma~\ref{lema8} (with $\ell=j_*$), in the case $k_i=0$ we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq88}
 n\in h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\end{equation}

Since $k_i\in\{0,1,\ldots,h\}$, the case $k_i=1$ is excluded by
\eqref{eq80}. By
\eqref{eq83} and \eqref{eq88}, in each of the other two cases we have
\(n\in h(A\setminus\{a\})\).
This completes the proof of the lemma.
head: environment

label: eq89
title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $A$ is a strongly minimal asymptotic basis of order $h$. By Lemma~\ref{lema7}, fix a constant $C>0$ such that
\[
 \left|W_j(m)-\frac mh\right|\leq C
 \qquad(1\leq j\leq h,\ m\geq0).
\]
In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq89}
 W_i(m)=\frac mh+O(1)
 \qquad(1\leq i\leq h).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
 K(m)=\max_{1\leq j\leq h}W_j(m)
 =\frac mh+O(1).
\]

Suppose that \eqref{eq3} fails. Then there exist
\[
 i\in\{1,\ldots,h\},
 \qquad
 w\in W_i,
\]
and
\[
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)
 \in\mathcal K_h\setminus\{(1,\ldots,1)\}
\]
such that, for every $t\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq90}
 \sum_{j=1}^hk_jP_j(t)
 \geq
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(t),&t\leq w,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle\sum_{j\neq i}P_j(t)+2^w,&t>w.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Let
\[
 a=2^w.
\]
Then
\(a\in A_i, \qquad {S}(a)=\{w\}\).
For any $M>w$, let
\[
 N_M=2^w+\sum_{\substack{0\leq t<M\\t\notin W_i}}2^t.
\]
By \eqref{eq90} and \eqref{eq12}, for every
$M>w$ and $1\leq r\leq M$ we have
\[
 N_M\bmod2^r\leq\sum_{j=1}^hk_jP_j(r).
\]
Since $0<N_M<2^M$, the representation criterion
\eqref{eq11} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq91}
 N_M\in\sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j.
\end{equation}

Fix $m>w$ and let
\[
 \mathcal H_m
 =\{0\leq n<2^m:{S}(n)\cap W_i=\{w\}\}.
\]
Let
\[
 \Omega_m=([0,m)\cap\mathbb Z)\setminus W_i.
\]
Then
\(\left|\Omega_m\right|=m-W_i(m)\).
For every $S\subseteq\Omega_m$, let
\(n_S=2^w+\sum_{t\in S}2^t\).
As $S(n_S)=\{w\}\sqcup S$, distinct subsets of $\Omega_m$
give distinct integers $n_S$. Moreover,
$\mathcal H_m=\{n_S:S\subseteq\Omega_m\}$.
Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq92}
 |\mathcal H_m|=2^{|\Omega_m|}=2^{m-W_i(m)}.
\end{equation}

For every $n\in\mathcal H_m$,
\begin{align*}
 {S}(n)
 &\subseteq
 \{w\}\sqcup\Omega_m\\
 &={S}(N_m).
\end{align*}
Applying \eqref{eq91} with $M=m$ and then Lemma~\ref{lema3}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq93}
 n\in\sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j
 \qquad(n\in\mathcal H_m).
\end{equation}

Let $L=L(h,C)$ be the integer in Lemma~\ref{lema9}. Let
\[
 q=\left\lfloor\frac{m-w-1}{L}\right\rfloor.
\]
For sufficiently large $m$, we have $q\geq1$. Define
\[
 I_r=[w+1+(r-1)L,w+1+rL)\cap\mathbb Z
 \qquad(1\leq r\leq q).
\]
Then
\begin{align*}
 \left|I_r\right|&=L,\\
 I_r\cap I_s&=\varnothing\qquad(r\neq s),\\
 \min I_r&>w=\max S(a),\\
 I_r&\subseteq[0,m).
\end{align*}
For $1\leq r\leq q$, let
\[
 J_r=I_r\setminus W_i,
 \qquad
 \ell_r=\left|J_r\right|.
\]
Then
\[
 0\leq\ell_r\leq L,
 \qquad
 J_r\cap J_s=\varnothing\quad(r\neq s).
\]
For $n\in\mathcal H_m$, let $\mathcal C_r(n)$ mean that
$S(n)\cap J_r=J_r$. Since $S(n)\cap W_i=\{w\}$ and
$\min I_r>w$, all binary digits of $n$ on $W_i\cap I_r$
are $0$. If $\mathcal C_r(n)$ holds, all digits on
$J_r=I_r\setminus W_i$ are $1$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq94}
 \varepsilon_t(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&t\in W_i\cap I_r,\\
 1,&t\in I_r\setminus W_i.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq93},
\[
 n\in\sum_{j=1}^hk_jB_j,
 \qquad
 (k_1,\ldots,k_h)\neq(1,\ldots,1).
\]
Therefore, whenever $\mathcal C_r(n)$ holds, Lemma~\ref{lema9} together with
\eqref{eq94} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq95}
 n\in h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\end{equation}

Now take
\(n\in E_a\cap\mathcal H_m\).
By $E_a=hA\setminus h(A\setminus\{a\})$,
\[
 n\notin h(A\setminus\{a\}).
\]
By \eqref{eq95}, $\mathcal C_r(n)$ fails for every
$1\leq r\leq q$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq1}
 E_a\cap\mathcal H_m
 \subseteq
 \{n\in\mathcal H_m:
 \mathcal C_r(n)\text{ fails for every }1\leq r\leq q\}.
\end{equation}

For each $r$, the $\ell_r$ digits in $J_r$ admit $2^{\ell_r}$
assignments, exactly one of which satisfies $\mathcal C_r$. Hence
\[
 \#\{(\varepsilon_t)_{t\in J_r}:\mathcal C_r(n)\text{ fails}\}
 =2^{\ell_r}-1.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 \frac{2^{\ell_r}-1}{2^{\ell_r}}
 &=1-2^{-\ell_r}\\
 &\leq1-2^{-L}.
\end{align*}
Let
\(J=\bigsqcup_{r=1}^qJ_r\).
Then
\begin{align*}
 \left|J\right|&=\sum_{r=1}^q\ell_r,\\
 \left|\Omega_m\setminus J\right|
 &=m-W_i(m)-\sum_{r=1}^q\ell_r.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left|\{n\in\mathcal H_m:
\mathcal C_r(n)\text{ fails for every }1\leq r\leq q\}\right|\\
&\quad=2^{\left|\Omega_m\setminus J\right|}
\prod_{r=1}^q(2^{\ell_r}-1)\\
&\quad=2^{m-W_i(m)-\sum_{r=1}^q\ell_r}
\prod_{r=1}^q(2^{\ell_r}-1)\\
&\quad=2^{m-W_i(m)}\prod_{r=1}^q(1-2^{-\ell_r})\\
&\quad\leq2^{m-W_i(m)}(1-2^{-L})^q.
\end{aligned}
\]
By \eqref{eq1},
\begin{align}
 \left|E_a\cap\mathcal H_m\right|
 &\leq
 2^{m-W_i(m)}(1-2^{-L})^q
 \nonumber\\
 &=
 2^{m-W_i(m)}
 (1-2^{-L})^{\lfloor(m-w-1)/L\rfloor}.
 \label{eq96}
\end{align}

Let
\[
 \rho=1-2^{-L}\in(0,1),
 \qquad
 \theta=\rho^{1/L}\in(0,1).
\]
By
\[
 q=\left\lfloor\frac{m-w-1}{L}\right\rfloor
 \geq\frac{m-w-1}{L}-1,
\]
we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \rho^q
 &\leq
 \rho^{(m-w-1)/L-1}\\
 &=\rho^{-1}\theta^{m-w-1}\\
 &=O_{w,L}(\theta^m)\\
 &=o(1).
\end{align*}
By \eqref{eq89},
\begin{align*}
 m-W_i(m)
 &=\frac{h-1}{h}m+O(1),\\
 2^{m-W_i(m)}
 &\asymp2^{(h-1)m/h}.
\end{align*}
Substituting these two estimates into \eqref{eq96}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq97}
 \left|E_a\cap\mathcal H_m\right|
 =o\bigl(2^{(h-1)m/h}\bigr).
\end{equation}

On the other hand, by Lemma~\ref{lema6},
\[
 \left|(E_a\cap[0,2^m))\setminus\mathcal H_m\right|
 =o\bigl(2^{(h-1)K(m)}\bigr).
\]
Combining this with $K(m)=m/h+O(1)$ yields
\[
 2^{(h-1)K(m)}
 =2^{(h-1)m/h+O(1)}\asymp2^{(h-1)m/h},
\]
so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq98}
 \left|(E_a\cap[0,2^m))\setminus\mathcal H_m\right|
 =o\bigl(2^{(h-1)m/h}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Moreover, since
\[
 E_a\cap[0,2^m)
 =
 (E_a\cap\mathcal H_m)
 \sqcup
 \bigl((E_a\cap[0,2^m))\setminus\mathcal H_m\bigr),
\]
we have, by \eqref{eq97} and \eqref{eq98},
\begin{align}
 E_a(2^m-1)
 &=\left|E_a\cap[0,2^m)\right|
 \nonumber\\
 &=o\bigl(2^{(h-1)m/h}\bigr).
 \label{eq99}
\end{align}

On the other hand, strong minimality gives a constant $c_a>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $m$,
\[
 E_a(2^m-1)
 \geq
 c_aA(2^m-1)^{h-1}.
\]
By \eqref{eq5} and \eqref{eq89},
$A(2^m-1)\asymp2^{m/h}$. Hence
\begin{align}
 E_a(2^m-1)
 &\gg_a A(2^m-1)^{h-1}
 \nonumber\\
 &\asymp2^{(h-1)m/h}.
 \label{eq100}
\end{align}
Therefore,
\[
 \frac{E_a(2^m-1)}{2^{(h-1)m/h}}
 \longrightarrow0,
\]
which contradicts
\[
 \frac{E_a(2^m-1)}{2^{(h-1)m/h}}
 \gg_a1.
\]
This contradiction establishes \eqref{eq3} for every
choice of $i$, $w$, and $(k_1,\ldots,k_h)$, and hence proves condition~(II).

Condition~(I) follows from \eqref{eq89}.
